_a_hole_this_ledger_does_not_inherit: test_certification_metadata.blocks() enumerates device blocks by looking for a device key or an environment.device_name, and complex_offdiag_update_e_2026-08-21 has neither -- it spells its device inside its host string, 'the GPU host, NVIDIA RTX A6000, CuPy 13.5.1'. So that block escapes the four-fact metadata requirement: 21 blocks found where 22 exist. rebind_cuda_welds.py.device_blocks adds a second discriminator -- a block whose named artifact directory holds a canonical policy leg is backed by a device run whether or not it says so -- which is how the block above is reported rather than silently missing. The record-side hole is not fixed here; fixing it means widening that enumerator, which is a change to a merge-bar test and belongs in its own pass.
_relation_to_certification_json: One record, two jobs, split by who writes them. certification.json is the NARRATIVE record: what each campaign measured, which mutations it caught, which numbers it produced, what it deliberately does not claim, and the certified/dead partition over the shipped kernels. It is written and revised by hand, it carries the reasoning, and it is the file to read to find out what a verdict means. fingerprints.json is the BINDING: for each of those campaigns, the artifact digest, the canonical policy legs, and the file-by-file digests of the sources the gate ran on, plus the live code identity of each of those files where it is still honest to record one. Every entry key here is the name of a certification.json block, which is the join between the two files.
_the_two_block_layout: Every entry has a mechanical block and a narrative block. The mechanical block is every key WITHOUT a leading underscore; rebind_cuda_welds.py owns all of it and rewrites all of it on every run. _notes is a nested object for bespoke prose; the tool writes it once, when it creates the entry, and never reads or rewrites it afterwards. Anything a person wants to say about an entry goes in there, where no tool will move it. This is the Metal ledger's discipline with its underscore-prefixed siblings gathered into one nested block, so 'did a tool write this?' is answered by where a key sits rather than by remembering a naming rule.
_what_is_absent_and_why: A block with no released verdict gets no entry. It is not listed as pending, partial, or expected -- absence is the claim. rebind_cuda_welds.py reports every such block by name each time it runs, so an absence stays visible without being recorded as a half-fact here.
_what_status_means: PASS: every canonical policy leg released, and every file this entry pins still matches the bytes the gate imported. DRIFTED: every leg still released -- the verdict stands on the run it describes -- but at least one pinned file has moved in the tree since, and those files are listed in source_drift. A DRIFTED entry owes a device re-run, and code_sha256 deliberately omits the moved files: code_identity.py licenses a weld to stand on an unchanged code digest only where source_sha256 still matches, 'because only then is the file on disk the bytes the gate actually ran', so backfilling a live code digest beside a stale source digest would manufacture the licence that clause withholds. CLEARED 2026-08-30: every entry here now reads PASS. All twenty campaigns were re-run on the GPU host into parity/meep_gpu/results/cuda_regate_2026-08-30/ (44 canonical policy legs, every one released) and rebound with rebind_cuda_welds.py --campaign. The re-gate tree is recorded by certification.json:cuda_regate_2026-08-30, written by record_cuda_regate.py; the dated family directories and their own artifact_sha256 values were not touched, because a record that disagrees with its own directory is worse than an honest drift. Each entry's campaign key names the block that records the run its digests came from.
_what_this_is: The hand-CUDA track's WELD LEDGER: one entry per released device campaign, each naming the sha256 of the tree files that campaign's gate imported. It is the sibling of metal_kernels/fingerprints.json and triton_kernels/fingerprints.json, and it is deliberately mechanical -- every entry in it was written by parity/meep_gpu/rebind_cuda_welds.py from an artifact, none was typed. It does NOT replace certification.json and does not repeat what that file says.
_which_blocks_are_absent_today: Measured 2026-08-28, the day this ledger was created: 22 certification.json blocks are backed by a device campaign and 20 have an entry here. The two without one are recut_2026-08-15, whose 2026-08-15 payloads predate canonical_verdict entirely, and complex_offdiag_update_e_2026-08-21, whose two policy legs carry canonical_verdict.released null. The second is the one that costs coverage: its two kernels, update_E_pml_complex_offdiag and update_E_no_pml_complex_offdiag, are the only 2 of the 48 names in the modules' CERTIFIED_KERNELS sets that no entry here welds. WHY THAT NULL IS THERE, corrected 2026-08-28 after the first reading of it was measured wrong: canonical_verdict is not the gate's own key. It is stamped beside the gate's spelling by the shared normaliser at parity/meep_gpu/gate_provenance.py:148, and read_verdict there recognises release-as-dict, released/passed/certifies bools, status and summary prose, verdict.{pass,passed,released,certified}, validation.status and all_ok/ok. This gate spells it verdict.release, one word off the nested-verdict branch, so the normaliser wrote 'no recognised verdict shape in this payload'. THE GATE DID STATE A RELEASE -- both legs carry verdict.release true over 18 clauses, all true, and the recomputed manifest digest d723b1cf876bc900... equals the artifact_sha256 the block records. So the earlier sentence here, that reading it would be 'inventing a verdict a gate declined to state', was wrong on both halves: the gate did not decline, and the null is the reader's, not the gate's. This ledger still does not weld the block, because widening a shared normaliser is a fleet-wide contract change with its own tests and its own owner, and because a wider reader would not change what is stamped in the artifact on disk. Two things close it, either of which is honest: widen read_verdict by the one spelling and re-stamp that gate, or re-cut it. Typing a verdict into this file is not one of them. RE-MEASURED 2026-08-30, after the re-gate: 23 family blocks are backed by a device campaign and 20 have an entry here, plus ONE block that is not a family at all -- cuda_regate_2026-08-30, whose re_gated table records the campaign that re-ran all twenty and whose verdict IS those twenty verdicts, so it owes no weld of its own and rebind_cuda_welds.py names it rather than reporting it absent. The three family blocks without an entry are recut_2026-08-15 and complex_offdiag_update_e_2026-08-21 as described above, and cuda_fused_magnetic_pair_2026-08-29_fillcarry, which is RELEASED and has simply never been seeded; it is reported by name on every run of the tool and closing it is a --seed away, held back here only because seeding a weld is a separate claim from re-binding twenty existing ones.
_which_is_authoritative_for_what: certification.json is authoritative for WHAT WAS CERTIFIED -- which kernels a campaign covers, under which policies, with what left open. Nothing here overrides it, and a kernel is certified only if a block there says so. fingerprints.json is authoritative for WHICH BYTES -- if the two disagree about a digest, this file is the one a tool recomputed from the artifact and the tree, and the disagreement is a re-run owed, not a number to edit. Neither file may be hand-corrected to make the other agree: the remedy is always re-running the gate and re-cutting the record from what it wrote.
_why_this_file_exists_at_all: certification.json pins the device SOURCE STRINGS a compiler is handed, which is a stronger claim than any Metal or Triton weld makes -- and it never pinned the HOST files that produce them. Measured 2026-08-28, when this ledger was created: 39 of the 79 files the 21 released blocks imported no longer matched the bytes their gate ran, and no clause anywhere said so, because there was nothing to say it with. Those 39 are not hidden here; each entry names its own in source_drift and reads status DRIFTED, which is what a weld is for.
